pillars.title: Fed liquidity
pillars.blurb: Cash the Fed leaves in the system after Treasury's account and money funds' parked cash.

core.name: Fed net liquidity
core.short: Fed balance sheet minus Treasury cash minus reverse repo
core.why: Proxy for cash the Fed leaves in the private system (≈ reserves + currency). Counts the TGA and RRP once.

members.name: Fed total assets
members.what: Total assets of the Federal Reserve (H.4.1).
members.why: Growing = QE adds reserves; shrinking = QT removes them.

members.name: Fed securities held outright
members.what: Treasuries and MBS the Fed owns.
members.why: Its 13-week change is the QT/QE pace.

members.name: Bank reserves at the Fed
members.what: Deposits banks hold at the Fed.
members.why: The core of money-market liquidity; scarce reserves force funding stress.

members.name: Treasury General Account (weekly)
members.what: Treasury's cash balance at the Fed (Wednesday).
members.why: When Treasury hoards cash, reserves fall; when it spends, they rise.

members.name: Treasury cash balance (daily)
members.what: TGA closing balance from the Daily Treasury Statement.
members.why: Same as weekly TGA but a few days fresher.

members.name: Overnight reverse repo
members.what: Money funds' cash parked at the Fed overnight.
members.why: Draining RRP released cash into markets in 2023–24; near zero it is no longer a buffer.

members.name: Fed repo operations (standing repo)
members.short: Emergency repo borrowing from the Fed
members.what: Repo lending by the Fed to dealers/banks.
members.why: Use spikes when private funding dries up.

members.name: Discount window primary credit
members.what: Banks' borrowing from the discount window.
members.why: Rises in bank stress (March 2023).

members.name: Bank Term Funding Program
members.what: Loans under the 2023 emergency bank facility.
members.why: History only — shows the 2023 bank-stress response. Program closed.

members.name: SOFR minus IORB
members.what: SOFR − IORB in basis points.
members.why: Above ~0 means reserves are no longer abundant (Sept 2019 spiked).

members.name: QT pace
members.what: 13-week change in securities held, monthly rate.
members.why: Negative = QT draining; positive = QE adding.

drivers: Last 13 weeks: net liquidity +$33bn. Biggest driver: Treasury cash (+$37bn).
Treasury cash +$37bn · Fed balance sheet −$4bn · Reverse repo $0bn
Reverse repo near empty: no buffer left to absorb QT or Treasury cash builds.
pillars.transmission: Reserves → bank and dealer balance sheets → money-market rates and risk appetite. Markets react within weeks; growth effects run through credit over 6–12 months.
pillars.classification: Creation/destruction. QE creates reserves; QT and Treasury cash builds destroy them. Reverse-repo drains release cash that already existed.
pillars.timing: Leading for risk assets (weeks to a quarter). Weak link to the economy on its own.

pillars.title: Government spending
pillars.blurb: How much the government spends beyond what it taxes, and how it funds the gap.

core.name: 12-month federal deficit
core.why: Government spending beyond taxes adds income and deposits to the private sector.

members.name: 12-month federal deficit
members.what: Rolling 12-month deficit ÷ nominal GDP.
members.why: Government spending beyond taxes adds income and deposits to the private sector.

members.name: Fiscal impulse
members.short: Is fiscal policy adding more or less?
members.what: 12-month change in the deficit as % of GDP.
members.why: Growth responds to the change in the deficit, not its level.

members.name: Federal surplus/deficit (monthly)
members.what: Monthly Treasury Statement surplus (+) or deficit (−).
members.why: Raw input to the 12-month deficit.

members.name: Personal transfer receipts
members.what: Social Security, Medicare, unemployment and other transfers.
members.why: Direct fiscal flow into household spending power.

members.name: Federal interest payments
members.what: Federal interest outlays.
members.why: Now a large income transfer to bondholders — stimulative for savers, a long-run fiscal risk.

members.name: Treasury bills outstanding
members.what: Marketable bills outstanding (MSPD, month-end).
members.why: Bill issuance is mostly funded by money funds (RRP cash) — less draining than coupons.

members.name: Treasury notes outstanding
members.what: Marketable notes outstanding (2–10y).
members.why: Coupon supply absorbs duration and bank deposits; pushes up term premium.

members.name: Treasury bonds outstanding
members.what: Marketable bonds outstanding (20–30y).
members.why: Long-duration supply the market must absorb.

members.name: Bill share of marketable debt
members.short: Share of debt in short-term bills
members.what: Bills ÷ total marketable debt.
members.why: Higher bill share = more liquidity-friendly financing; Treasury's "stealth QE" lever.

drivers: Deficit 6.4% of GDP over the last 12 months; up 0.7pp on a year ago (more support).
Net issuance, last 3 months: bills +$393bn, notes+bonds +$239bn. Bills are 23.0% of marketable debt.
Federal interest costs $1.33tn a year (annual rate), +7.3% y/y — income to bondholders.
Treasury cash balance $891bn (2026-11-19) — counted in Fed liquidity.
pillars.transmission: Deficit spending lands as household and business income and deposits. Coupon issuance competes for savings and pushes up long yields; bills mostly draw idle money-fund cash.
pillars.classification: Adds private-sector income and deposits (net financial assets). Funding mix decides how much is offset: bills ≈ neutral, coupons absorb duration and deposits.
pillars.timing: Leading for growth by 2–4 quarters (impulse). Level matters less than the change.

pillars.title: Bank lending
pillars.blurb: Banks create new money when they lend. This is the main private source of new liquidity.

core.name: Bank credit
core.what: Loans and securities held by all commercial banks (H.8).
core.why: When banks extend credit they create deposits — new money.

members.name: Bank credit
members.what: Loans and securities held by all commercial banks (H.8).
members.why: When banks extend credit they create deposits — new money.

members.name: Bank loans and leases
members.what: Total loans and leases at commercial banks.
members.why: The lending part of bank credit.

members.name: Commercial & industrial loans
members.what: C&I loans at commercial banks.
members.why: Business borrowing; lags the cycle but confirms turns.

members.name: Commercial real estate loans
members.what: CRE loans at commercial banks.
members.why: Key bank exposure; weak office values constrain lending.

members.name: Consumer loans
members.what: Consumer loans at commercial banks.
members.why: Household borrowing via banks.

members.name: Credit card loans
members.what: Credit card and revolving loans at banks.
members.why: Fast growth can mean households are borrowing to keep spending.

members.name: Bank loans to nonbank financials
members.short: Bank loans to private credit & other lenders
members.what: Loans to nondepository financial institutions (funds, BDCs, finance cos).
members.why: Bank money flowing into private credit — the link between banks and shadow lending. Counted here, not in private credit.

members.name: Bank deposits
members.what: Deposits at commercial banks.
members.why: Funding base for lending; overlaps with M2 (not added).

members.name: M2 money supply
members.what: Cash, deposits and money funds held by the public.
members.why: Broad money; shown, not added, because it overlaps bank credit.

members.name: Loan officers tightening business loans
members.what: Net % of banks tightening C&I standards (SLOOS).
members.why: Tightening leads loan growth and defaults by 2–4 quarters.

members.name: Business loan demand
members.what: Net % of banks reporting stronger C&I loan demand.
members.why: Separates supply (standards) from demand.

members.name: Loan officers tightening credit cards
members.what: Net % of banks tightening card standards.
members.why: Tighter cards hit lower-income spending first.

drivers: Bank credit impulse +0.88pp of GDP (change in the yearly credit flow).
Loan growth, last 13 weeks annualised: Nonbank lenders (private credit etc.) +20.5% · Business (C&I) +13.7% · Commercial real estate +5.0% · Credit cards +4.0% · Consumer +3.2%
Net 2% of banks tightening business-loan standards (2026 Q4).
pillars.transmission: Looser standards → more loans → new deposits → spending and investment. Standards lead loan growth by 2–4 quarters.
pillars.classification: Creation. Bank lending creates deposits. Deposits and M2 are shown but not added (they are the other side of the same loans). Bank loans to private-credit funds count here only.
pillars.timing: Standards: leading (2–4 quarters). Loan volumes: coincident to lagging.

pillars.title: Private credit & bonds
pillars.blurb: Credit from bond markets, private-credit funds and other non-banks. Mostly moves existing savings around.

core.name: Baa corporate spread
core.why: Price of credit; widening = lenders pulling back. Back to 1986, so usable for history.

members.name: Baa corporate spread
members.what: Moody's Baa yield minus 10-year Treasury.
members.why: Price of credit; widening = lenders pulling back. Back to 1986, so usable for history.

members.name: High-yield spread
members.what: ICE BofA US high-yield option-adjusted spread.
members.why: Most sensitive public credit gauge. FRED carries only ~3 years.

members.name: Investment-grade spread
members.what: ICE BofA US corporate (IG) OAS.
members.why: Funding cost for most large borrowers, including AI capex issuers.

members.name: CCC spread
members.what: ICE BofA CCC & lower OAS.
members.why: First place stress shows.

members.name: Corporate bonds outstanding
members.what: Nonfinancial corporate debt securities (Fed Z.1).
members.why: Growth = companies raising money in bond markets (mostly redistributes savings).

members.name: Corporate debt (bonds + loans)
members.what: Nonfinancial corporate debt securities and loans (Z.1).
members.why: Includes bank loans already counted in banking — shown only.

members.name: Commercial paper outstanding
members.what: Commercial paper outstanding.
members.why: Short-term funding market; collapses in panics (2008).

members.name: BDC index ETF
members.what: Price of a basket of listed BDCs.
members.why: Only daily market price on direct lending; falls when private credit losses are feared.

members.name: Ares Capital
members.what: Share price of the largest BDC.
members.why: Bellwether for direct lending sentiment.

members.name: Senior loan ETF
members.what: Price of a broadly syndicated leveraged loan ETF.
members.why: Floating-rate loan market; stress shows here and in private credit together.

members.name: High-yield bond ETF
members.what: Price of a high-yield bond ETF.
members.why: Tradable HY proxy with long history.

members.name: IG corporate bond ETF
members.what: Price of an investment-grade bond ETF.
members.why: Tradable IG proxy.

members.name: Blackstone
members.what: Share price of the largest alternatives manager.
members.why: Market's read on private equity and credit fundraising.

drivers: Warning: high-yield spreads up 106bp in 13 weeks — fast widening often comes before broader credit stress.
High-yield spread 3.76% (+106bp over 13 weeks; 96th percentile of 3 years).
Investment-grade spread 0.98% (+17bp over 13 weeks; 87th percentile of 3 years).
Baa spread 1.56% (−8bp over 13 weeks; 6th percentile of 20 years).
No daily private-credit prices (Tiingo key not working) — using public spreads only.
Corporate bonds outstanding +4.1% y/y (2026 Q2).
pillars.transmission: Tight spreads and open markets let weaker borrowers refinance; when spreads widen, refinancing stops and defaults follow 2–4 quarters later.
pillars.classification: Mostly redistribution: investors' existing savings are lent on. The bank-funded slice (bank loans to nonbank lenders) is counted under Bank lending, not here. Spreads measure whether the channel is open.
pillars.timing: Spreads: leading to coincident. Volumes: lagging.

pillars.title: Global liquidity
pillars.blurb: Liquidity from other central banks and the price of dollars abroad.

core.name: ECB + BoJ balance sheets in USD
core.what: ECB + BoJ assets converted at market FX; Fed excluded (counted in central bank pillar).
core.why: Non-US central bank liquidity in dollar terms; change split into local growth vs FX.

core.name: Broad dollar index
core.why: A rising dollar tightens global dollar funding and hurts non-US borrowers.

members.name: ECB + BoJ balance sheets in USD
members.what: ECB + BoJ assets converted at market FX; Fed excluded (counted in central bank pillar).
members.why: Non-US central bank liquidity in dollar terms; change split into local growth vs FX.

members.name: ECB total assets
members.what: Eurosystem total assets.
members.why: Euro liquidity; input to the global balance-sheet total.

members.name: BoJ total assets
members.what: Bank of Japan total assets.
members.why: Yen liquidity and carry-trade funding.

members.name: Broad dollar index
members.what: Fed's broad trade-weighted dollar.
members.why: A rising dollar tightens global dollar funding and hurts non-US borrowers.

members.name: JPY per USD
members.what: Yen per dollar.
members.why: Weak yen fuels carry trades; sharp yen rallies unwind them (Aug 2024).

members.name: CNY per USD
members.what: Yuan per dollar.
members.why: PBOC's managed currency; weakening = capital outflow pressure.

members.name: China FX reserves
members.what: China total reserves excluding gold.
members.why: Best free proxy for PBOC foreign-asset liquidity; PBOC balance sheet not freely available in clean form.

members.name: Fed FX swap lines
members.short: Dollars lent to foreign central banks
members.what: Central bank liquidity swaps outstanding.
members.why: Jumps only in global dollar shortages (2008, 2020).

members.name: Foreign official Treasury custody
members.short: Foreign central banks' Treasuries at the Fed
members.what: Treasuries held at the NY Fed for foreign officials.
members.why: Falling = foreign officials selling Treasuries (often to defend currencies).

members.name: Foreign repo pool
members.short: Foreign central banks' cash at the Fed
members.what: Reverse repos with foreign official accounts.
members.why: Dollar cash held back by foreign officials.

members.name: USD credit to non-US borrowers
members.what: BIS global liquidity — USD bank loans and bonds to non-bank borrowers outside the US.
members.why: Offshore dollar credit growth = easier global dollar liquidity.

drivers: ECB + BoJ balance sheets $10.54tn in dollars; 13-week change −$345bn = balance sheets −$127bn + currency moves −$217bn.
Dollar +3.1% over 13 weeks (tighter global dollar conditions).
Foreign central banks' Treasuries at the Fed −$42bn over 13 weeks.
pillars.transmission: Foreign easing and a weaker dollar loosen global funding and push capital into risk assets, including US ones. A strong dollar squeezes non-US dollar borrowers and EM.
pillars.classification: Creation abroad (ECB/BoJ assets) plus the price of dollar funding. The Fed is excluded here to avoid double counting. PBOC is proxied by China's FX reserves.
pillars.timing: Leading for risk assets and EM (1–2 quarters).

pillars.title: AI investment
pillars.blurb: Where AI spending comes from and where the money goes.

core.name: Hyperscaler capex (5 firms)
core.what: Sum of quarterly capex for MSFT, GOOGL, AMZN, META, ORCL.
core.why: Largest single private investment cycle; mostly funded from cash flow (redistribution, not new money).

members.name: Hyperscaler capex (5 firms)
members.what: Sum of quarterly capex for MSFT, GOOGL, AMZN, META, ORCL.
members.why: Largest single private investment cycle; mostly funded from cash flow (redistribution, not new money).

members.name: Office & data center construction
members.what: Private office construction spending (Census includes data centers).
members.why: Physical data-center buildout; office alone is falling, so growth here is data centers.

members.name: Power construction
members.what: Private power construction spending.
members.why: Power is the binding constraint on AI buildout.

members.name: Manufacturing construction
members.what: Private manufacturing construction spending.
members.why: Chip fabs and reshoring.

members.name: Information processing equipment investment
members.what: Nominal private investment in information processing equipment (GDP).
members.why: Where AI servers show up in GDP.

members.name: Computer & electronics orders
members.what: New orders, computers and electronic products.
members.why: Leads equipment investment.

members.name: Semiconductor output
members.what: Industrial production of semiconductors and components.
members.why: Domestic chip output.

members.name: Semiconductor ETF
members.what: Price of a semiconductor equity ETF.
members.why: Market's verdict on the AI capex cycle.

drivers: Big Tech capex $230bn in 2026Q3, +118% y/y.
Capex is 116% of their operating cash flow; 86% funded internally.
Debt raised over the last 4 quarters: $272bn (vs capex $691bn).
Office/data-center construction +39.5% y/y (Sep 2026).
Power construction +12.1% y/y (Sep 2026).
Not captured: off-balance-sheet structures (e.g. joint-venture data centers funded by private credit, operating leases not yet started). These move debt off hyperscaler balance sheets.
pillars.transmission: Capex flows to chipmakers, equipment, construction, utilities and power. It lifts GDP and earnings in those industries; it does not add much new money to the system.
pillars.classification: Mostly redistribution: funded from cash flow (existing corporate cash). Bond issuance moves investors' savings to hyperscalers. New credit is created only where banks lend (counted under Bank lending). Leases and joint ventures move risk off balance sheets.
pillars.timing: Coincident for GDP and industrial demand; earnings of suppliers lead the capex itself.

rules: Pillars are combined as standardised impulses (direction and speed), never by adding dollar amounts.
Dollar totals are shown only where units match: Fed net liquidity, and ECB + BoJ in dollars.
Treasury cash and reverse repo are counted once, inside Fed net liquidity — not again under fiscal.
Bank reserves are shown but not added to net liquidity (they are mostly the same money).
Deposits and M2 are shown but not added to bank credit (they are the other side of the same loans).
Bank loans to private-credit funds count under Bank lending, not Private credit.
The Fed is excluded from Global liquidity because it is already counted in Fed liquidity.
AI capex funded from cash flow or bonds is redistribution, not new liquidity.
Stale pillars are left out of the composite and listed.
consolidated.split_note: Pillars are grouped by what they lead, as classified before testing: market liquidity (Fed, global, credit spreads) for risk assets; economy liquidity (deficits, bank lending, AI capex) for growth. The back-test (Research tab) shows market liquidity lining up with stock returns far better than the all-pillar average, which the economy pillars dilute.

analogues.summary: The 5 closest past months saw stocks +4% (median) over the next 12 months (range -6% to +22%). History rhymes; it does not repeat.
analogues.method: Monthly features standardised over 1986–today; distance = root-mean-square gap across available features; months within 2 years of today excluded; one pick per 12-month window.

principles.test: When market liquidity is clearly positive (negative), are the next 6 months' stock returns above (below) average? Compared with the all-pillar and economy composites.
principles.plain: Market liquidity since 2002-06: stocks rose 9.18% in the 6 months after a positive reading vs 1.06% after a negative one; it picked above-average periods 67.9% of the time. The all-pillar average managed 43.4% and the economy pillars 43.5% — liquidity works for markets only when measured the right way. Long-history money/credit proxy (since 1989-06): 58.4%.

principles.principle: Direction and acceleration matter more than level
principles.test: Correlation of Fed net liquidity (level vs 3m change vs change in change) with next-6m stock returns.
principles.plain: Correlations with next-6m returns — level +0.20, change -0.02, acceleration -0.17. Strongest: level. All are weak in absolute terms.

principles.test: At which horizon does the long-history liquidity proxy best line up with stocks and with the economy?
principles.plain: Liquidity lines up best with stocks 12m ahead and with industrial output 12m ahead. Both peak at similar horizons here; the 12–18-month lens holds for the economy.

principles.principle: Credit exposes weakness before the economy does
principles.test: Before each recession since 1990, did Baa spreads widen (6m change > 0.4pp) before the Sahm rule fired?
principles.plain: Credit spreads warned a median 10 months before recessions began; the jobs-based Sahm rule fired a median 1 month(s) after they began. Widening spreads lead rising unemployment by ~1 months.

principles.principle: Opportunities come when markets and liquidity disagree
principles.test: Next-6m returns when stocks rallied despite draining liquidity, and when they fell despite improving liquidity.
principles.plain: After sell-offs into improving liquidity, stocks returned +8.7% over 6 months (n=9) vs +5.1% on average; after rallies into draining liquidity, +2.4% (n=5). Small samples.

principles.principle: Central-bank stress and side effects create opportunities
principles.test: Stock returns in the 6 months after the Fed's emergency facilities were first tapped.
principles.plain: 11 stress events; median next-6m stock return +3.3%. Buying stress worked when the Fed responded fast (2019, 2020, 2023), not in 2008.

thesis: The economy is in expansion. Market liquidity is neutral and stable; economy liquidity is adding and deteriorating.
Inflation is broad-driven: core PCE 3.1% a year, 2.9% annualised lately — the Fed's room to ease is limited.
Consumers: spending is outrunning real income; households are saving less to keep spending.
Risk is poorly paid in US equities, Corporate credit. Better paid: Long Treasuries, Real yields.
Most favoured by the framework: Cash, Government bonds. Least favoured: Investment-grade credit, International equities.

Corporate credit: Baa spread over Treasuries 1.56%
